summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime, Galina Lebedev, Jackline Abo-Nassar, Sally Marzouk, Moshe Inbar, Murad Ghanim, Radi Aly
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the biological activity of crude extracts from Ajuga iva against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The research focuses on the potential of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes, natural compounds found in Ajuga plants, as green alternatives to synthetic pesticides. The authors hypothesized that these compounds, which mimic insect molting hormones, would disrupt larval development and survival. Using first and third instar larvae, the study demonstrated that A. iva crude leaf extract significantly increased mortality, reduced larval weight gain (LWG), and decreased relative growth rate (RGR) in a dose-dependent manner. Specifically, the highest concentration (250 µg/µl) resulted in 85% mortality in first instars and prevented pupation in third instars. Histological analysis using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed severe gut damage, including nuclear abnormalities and reduced actin filament organization, suggesting a direct toxic effect on gut epithelial cells. The study also confirmed that purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) isolated from the extract retained significant biological activity, causing similar developmental disruptions. In contrast, commercial standards at low concentrations showed no significant effect, highlighting the potency of the plant-derived mixture. The findings support the use of A. iva extracts in Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, offering a safer, environmentally friendly option for controlling S. littoralis while minimizing risks to human health and the environment.

claims.description: Ajuga iva crude leaf extract significantly reduces the survival and development of Spodoptera littoralis larvae.
Phytoecdysteroids in A. iva cause direct damage to the larval gut.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the biological activity of crude extracts from Ajuga iva against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The research focuses on the potential of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes, natural compounds found in Ajuga plants, as green alternatives to synthetic pesticides. The authors hypothesized that these compounds, which mimic insect molting hormones, would disrupt larval development and survival. Using first and third instar larvae, the study demonstrated that A. iva crude leaf extract significantly increased mortality, reduced larval weight gain (LWG), and decreased relative growth rate (RGR) in a dose-dependent manner. Specifically, the highest concentration (250 µg/µl) resulted in 85% mortality in first instars and prevented pupation in third instars. Histological analysis using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed severe gut damage, including nuclear abnormalities and reduced actin filament organization, suggesting a direct toxic effect on gut epithelial cells. The study also confirmed that purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) isolated from the extract retained significant biological activity, causing similar developmental disruptions. In contrast, commercial standards at low concentrations showed no significant effect, highlighting the potency of the plant-derived mixture. The findings support the use of A. iva extracts in Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, offering a safer, environmentally friendly option for controlling S. littoralis while minimizing risks to human health and the environment.

Research Context
Insects cause severe damage to crops, and current control methods rely on pesticides with negative environmental impacts. Green control is gaining popularity due to concerns about pesticide side effects. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroids that mimic insect molting hormones. These compounds are present in 5-6% of plant species at higher concentrations than in arthropods. Ajuga plants contain high levels of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes. Previous studies showed Ajuga extracts inhibit ecdysis and cause mortality in other pests. The study aims to evaluate A. iva extracts against Spodoptera littoralis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether A. iva crude leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae. A second question examines if isolated phytoecdysteroids have different effects than the crude extract. A third question investigates if phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut. The hypothesis is that A. iva extracts containing phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes are promising pest-control agents. It is predicted that these compounds will interfere with molting and metamorphosis. The study expects the extracts to reduce damage caused by S. littoralis larvae.

Methodological Details
Young and mature leaves and stems of A. iva were collected after blooming. Plant material was oven-dried at 55°C for 3-4 days and homogenized. Crude extracts were prepared by soaking 24 g of powder in 240 ml MeOH. The extract was homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 hour and centrifuged. LC-TOF-MS was used to identify phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes in three concentrations. First and third instar S. littoralis larvae were reared on castor bean leaves. Larvae were exposed to 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl of crude leaf extract. Experiments were conducted in a climate-controlled room at 25°C. Gut morphology was analyzed using DAPI and phalloidin staining. Statistical analyses included t-tests, mixed-model ANOVA, and Friedman tests.

Procedures And Architectures
Castor bean leaves were smeared with aqueous A. iva crude leaf extract. Tween 20 was added as a surfactant to the extract solution. Treated leaves were dried in a chemical hood for 2 hours. First instar larvae were placed on treated leaves for 3 days. Third instar larvae were fed on treated leaves for 4 or 8 days. Freshly treated leaves were provided after 4 days to avoid decay. Larval mortality, survival, and relative growth rate were recorded. Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days. Guts were dissected, fixed in paraformaldehyde, and stained. Images were captured using Leica and Olympus confocal microscopes.

Key Results
First instar larvae showed significant mortality increases at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. Mortality rates were 25%, 65%, and 85% respectively, compared to 5% in controls. Third instar larvae showed reduced larval weight gain at all concentrations. Relative growth rate was significantly decreased compared to controls. At 250 µg/µl, RGR decreased by 0.05 and 0.20 g/g day on days 6 and 8. None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days at the highest concentration. Purified phytoecdysteroid mixture also significantly reduced RGR and survival. Larvae fed on 250 µg/µl extract or phytoecdysteroid mixture lost weight and died. Gut nuclei were smaller and abnormally shaped in treated larvae. Actin filaments were smaller and reduced in amount in treated guts. Treated larvae were unable to complete pupation after 15 days.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results support the hypothesis that A. iva extracts disrupt S. littoralis development. Phytoecdysteroids likely interfere with molting and metamorphosis processes. Gut damage suggests a direct toxic effect on epithelial cells. Reduced growth and weight gain prevent larvae from reaching pupation threshold. The findings align with previous studies on phytoecdysteroid toxicity in insects. A. iva extracts offer a potential green control method for IPM programs.

Claims
Ajuga iva crude leaf extract significantly reduces the survival and development of Spodoptera littoralis larvae. Mortality increased to 85% at the highest concentration. Relative growth rate was significantly decreased. Larvae were unable to pupate. Commercial standards at 100 ppm had no significant effect. A. iva extracts are promising for pest control.
Phytoecdysteroids in A. iva cause direct damage to the larval gut. Gut nuclei were abnormally shaped. Actin filaments were reduced in amount.  Gut damage contributes to larval mortality.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used multiple concentrations to assess dose-dependency. Purified phytoecdysteroids were tested to confirm specific activity. Control treatments with water and Tween 20 were included.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TLC analysis of phytoecdysteroids. Figure 2 displays larval mortality and weight gain. Figure 3 illustrates relative growth rate and survival. Figure 4 shows the effect of treatment order. Figure 5 presents the effect of purified phytoecdysteroids. Figure 6 shows gut histology with DAPI and phalloidin. Figure 7 depicts incomplete pupae.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating the efficacy of A. iva extracts against S. littoralis. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-dependent mortality and gut damage. 3. The future path is the integration of A. iva into IPM programs.
